extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers and practitioners seeking an overview of COVID-19 misinformation and approaches to counter it
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and classify misinformation about COVID-19: its types, actors, channels, amplifying factors, harms, and countermeasures, as presented in an encyclopedic overview. Useful for informing fact-checking, media literacy, and public-health communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of misinformation (reconfiguration vs fabrication; top‑down)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most misinformation related to COVID-19 involves 'various forms of reconfiguration, where existing and often true information is spun, twisted, recontextualised, or reworked'; less misinformation 'was completely fabricated'. 'Top‑down misinformation from politicians, celebrities, and other prominent public figures' captured a majority of social media engagement despite accounting for a minority of samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify claims by whether they rework true information or are outright fabrications; track whether a claim is propagated top‑down by influential actors (which drives engagement) or bottom‑up. Use Reuters Institute classification referenced in the article as an example of this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms/tactics of disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics used include astroturfing, big lie, circular reporting, clickbait, conspiracy theorizing, doublespeak, fear/uncertainty/doubt (FUD), forgery, cherry picking, false attribution/balance, Gish gallop, quote mining, and other listed manipulative techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating content, look for these tactics as signals of coordinated or manipulative messaging. The article lists many named tactics (e.g., 'firehose of falsehood', 'clickbait', 'cherry picking') which can be used as a checklist when auditing messages or platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels and sources of spread
rubrics_metrics.description: False information has been spread through social media, text messaging, mass media (television and radio), preprint servers, celebrities, politicians, public figures, and state actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both the medium (social networks, private chats, broadcast) and the source (individual influencers, media outlets, governments). Note that different channels have different moderation levers and different audience dynamics (e.g., private chats are harder to moderate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplifying factors for misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplifiers include cognitive biases (jumping to conclusions, confirmation bias), uncertainty among experts combined with lay misunderstanding of scientific process, preprint dissemination without peer review, political motives, nationalism, echo chambers, and high‑engagement from celebrities or politicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging why a claim spread, examine these social and cognitive factors. Mitigation strategies should address specific amplifiers (e.g., improving scientific literacy to counter misunderstanding of preprints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating scientific/origin claims about the virus
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific evaluation should rely on genomic evidence and peer‑reviewed research; the consensus among virologists (per the article) is that natural zoonotic spillover is most likely, while laboratory origins are considered unlikely given current evidence. 'Genetic manipulation has been ruled out by genomic analysis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use genomic analyses, transparency of data, peer‑reviewed studies, and scientific consensus as primary standards. Treat unreviewed preprints, ad hoc claims, or politically motivated statements with caution; request reproducible evidence and expert assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific evidence standards (peer review and consensus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers on preprint servers are uploaded without peer review or editorial quality control; some preprints have contributed to spreading conspiracy theories. Majority of peer‑reviewed research points to a natural origin; peer review and consensus are invoked repeatedly as standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize peer‑reviewed, reproducible studies and statements of scientific consensus when assessing technical claims. Flag and contextualise preprints to avoid amplification of unverified findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility check against known science (example: 5G claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be consistent with established scientific facts (e.g., 'Viruses cannot be transmitted by radio waves'); implausible mechanisms (like 5G causing viral infection) are flagged and debunked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply simple domain‑consistency tests: is the mechanism consistent with biology/physics? If not, classify as false. Use authoritative fact‑checks and scientific statements to rebut implausible mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public‑health and societal harm metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Harms from COVID‑19 misinformation include increased infection and death rates (linked to reduced adherence to public‑health guidance), vaccine hesitancy, distrust of news organisations and medical authorities, divisiveness, political fragmentation, threats and violence (e.g., arson attacks on 5G masts), and bullying of scientists and public officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the severity of misinformation, measure epidemiological outcomes (vaccination uptake, infection/death rates), social outcomes (trust, polarization), and incidents of real‑world harm (violence, arrests). Use studies cited (e.g., natural experiment on Fox News exposure) as models for linking misinformation to outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and actor intent (propaganda and information operations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some misinformation originates from state‑backed operations or government spokespeople; motivations include political advantage, scapegoating, undermining democratic debate, or promoting governmental models. The article documents accusations of state propaganda (e.g., Russia, China) and organised online influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether messaging is organic or part of coordinated state influence (look for patterns across many accounts, repeated narratives, amplification networks). Consider geopolitical motives and whether messaging aligns with state narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media responsibility and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast and print media can propagate misinformation; regulatory bodies (e.g., Ofcom) criticised ambiguous or ill‑judged comments that risk undermining public trust. Journalistic practices (verification, avoiding false balance) affect spread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate media content for verification, sourcing, balance (avoid false balance), and potential to cause public harm. Regulatory findings and corrections/retractions are relevant evidence of media failure to meet standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter‑misinformation methods (toolbox)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods to counter disinformation include academic research, critical thinking, digital literacy, health literacy, information literacy, media literacy, science communication, promoting scientific consensus and scientific literacy, 'truth sandwich' technique, watchdog journalism, fact‑checking, community notes, content moderation, and platform policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy a mix of education (literacy programs), remediation (fact‑checks, truth sandwiches), platform interventions (moderation, de‑recommendation), and research. The article lists these as established approaches — use them as a checklist when designing countermeasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform and policy levers (content moderation and de‑promotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms have specific levers: remove or reduce reach of content (e.g., YouTube reducing content linking 5G and COVID‑19), remove or label borderline content, and adjust recommendations. Speed of action matters (example: YouTube took on average 41 days to remove Covid‑related videos in early 2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess platform responses on timeliness, consistency, and the specific interventions used (removal, de‑recommendation, labeling). Measure effectiveness by reductions in views/engagement and downstream harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of fact‑checking and watchdog organisations
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent fact‑checking organisations, watchdog journalism, and non‑profits (e.g., Full Fact, FactCheck.org, Reuters fact checks) are named as resources for debunking and tracking misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reputable fact‑checks to verify claims and to provide sourced rebuttals. Track which organisations have assessed a claim and their evidence; incorporate fact‑check results into public communication and platform moderation decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of target audiences and campaign goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Misinformation targets audiences for diverse goals: to avoid responsibility, scapegoat, influence elections, sow distrust, profit commercially (scams), or incite violence. Certain demographic or partisan audiences may be more susceptible (example: areas with higher Trump vote shares had lower vaccination rates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing a campaign, identify the intended audience and likely objective (political influence, financial scam, social disruption). Tailor countermeasures to audience characteristics (language, platform preference, trust anchors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples and case studies as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The article uses case studies (Fox News programming natural experiment, 5G mast arson incidents, viral preprints, public figures' statements) to illustrate mechanisms and impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluation or reporting, include concrete case studies linking content to outcomes. Use well‑documented incidents to support causal claims and to design targeted interventions.
